content: None of the included studies reported cases of neonatal sepsis. Other critical outcomes were either not reported or had no events recorded. When comparing cephalosporins to penicillins by type of cesarean section, most trials included women undergoing either elective or emergency cesarean sections. In terms of timing of antibiotic administration, all but two trials administered antibiotics before umbilical cord clamping. Two trials did not report the timing of antibiotic administration. Regarding the route of administration, twenty trials compared antibiotics given intravenously, while two studies compared antibiotics administered as a lavage or irrigation during surgery. Two small trials tested ciprofloxacin versus ampicillin/sulbactam or cefotetan. No differences were found between these antibiotics in terms of maternal sepsis, endometritis, or wound infection. Other antibiotic regimens compared to penicillin or cephalosporins also showed no significant differences in outcomes such as wound infection and endometritis. One trial compared gentamicin (an aminoglycoside) plus metronidazole (a nitroimidazole) with a standard antibiotic cocktail containing penicillin, nitroimidazole, and macrolide. No maternal deaths or nephrotoxicity were observed. Two trials compared short versus long durations of treatment. In one trial, women in the intervention arm received no further treatment after delivery, while the control arm continued intrapartum antibiotics postpartum until they were afebrile and asymptomatic for 24 hours. In the second trial, women in the short-course arm received a single dose of cefotetan within one hour of delivery, while those in the long-course arm received cefotetan every 12 hours for at least 48 hours. The overall quality of evidence was graded as very low. There is insufficient evidence to determine the most appropriate antimicrobial regimen for treating intra-amniotic infection or whether antibiotics should be continued postpartum. Available trials were generally small and underpowered to detect statistical differences between regimens. First-generation cephalosporins and penicillin are cost-effective and widely available options for prophylaxis in cesarean sections. However, healthcare providers and policymakers may vary in their choice of antibiotics based on local bacterial resistance patterns, availability, and cost. For the treatment of chorioamnionitis, a simple regimen such as ampicillin and once-daily gentamicin is recommended as first-line therapy. This recommendation is conditional and based on very low-quality evidence. The regimen is favored for its simplicity, short duration, and adherence to principles of antibiotic stewardship to reduce the emergence of resistant bacterial strains. For postpartum endometritis, a combination of clindamycin and gentamicin is recommended. However, in low-resource settings where clindamycin may not be available or affordable, penicillin-class drugs are suggested as an alternative. Treatment duration should continue as long as clinical symptoms and signs persist. Evidence on the use of different antibiotic regimens for postpartum endometritis was extracted from a Cochrane systematic review. Trials were mostly conducted in high-income countries, particularly the USA. Clinical criteria for defining endometritis included fever and uterine tenderness, with some trials also considering pelvic pain, purulent lochia, and leukocytosis. No trials reported maternal mortality, and long-term complications such as subfertility or uterine adhesions were not considered. In trials comparing gentamicin plus penicillin or ampicillin versus other regimens, no severe complications, diarrhea, or allergic reactions were reported. Similarly, no significant differences were found in side effects or hospital stay length among various antibiotic regimens. Two trials compared cephalosporins with longer half-lives to those with shorter half-lives, such as cefotetan versus cefmetazole or cefotetan versus cefoxitin. No significant differences in outcomes were observed. One trial compared metronidazole plus gentamicin to penicillins (ampicillin plus sulbactam) and found no significant differences in outcomes. Four studies compared once-daily versus thrice-daily gentamicin administration, with no significant differences in outcomes. Three trials tested continued oral antibiotics after an intravenous course versus no further treatment. No significant differences in outcomes were observed.
